spark.summary: Isolation levels control which concurrent read/write anomalies a database permits, trading throughput and lock/abort rates for correctness—while distributed ACID extends those guarantees across shards via 2PC, TrueTime, or HLCs.
spark.keyTakeaway: PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ is Snapshot Isolation (still vulnerable to Write Skew), not true Serializability; across shards, distributed ACID requires either 2PC + SSI/TrueTime commit-wait or deterministic ordering—and retry loops for 40001 serialization failures.

concept.whyItMatters: Default `READ COMMITTED` isolation lets two concurrent transfers check `balance >= $100` simultaneously and both withdraw, leaving a negative balance. Even upgrading to `REPEATABLE READ` (Snapshot Isolation) in PostgreSQL still allows **Write Skew**—for example, two on-call doctors both checking that 2 doctors are on shift and both signing off at the same time, leaving 0 on call. In distributed databases (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB), preserving ACID across shards adds cross-node clock uncertainty and network round-trips that directly impact p99 tail latency.
whenToUse: Financial ledgers, double-entry accounting, and inventory/seat reservations where lost updates, phantom reads, or write skew violate business invariants.
Multi-shard writes in CockroachDB, Google Spanner, or YugabyteDB where cross-partition atomicity and external consistency (linearizability) are required.
Read-heavy analytics or billing snapshots (`REPEATABLE READ`) that need a consistent point-in-time view across multiple tables without blocking concurrent writers.
whenNotToUse: High-contention counters (like post view counts or rate-limiters) where `SERIALIZABLE` triggers 30%+ `40001` aborts—use atomic `UPDATE ... SET count = count + 1`, Redis `INCR`, or sharded counters.

Multi-service workflows spanning external HTTP APIs (Stripe, Twilio) where holding distributed locks across network calls causes cascading timeouts; use the Saga + Transactional Outbox pattern instead.
Append-only telemetry or event logs where `READ COMMITTED` suffices and zero-coordination throughput is the priority.
keyPoints: ANSI SQL-92 defines 4 levels (`READ UNCOMMITTED`, `READ COMMITTED`, `REPEATABLE READ`, `SERIALIZABLE`) around Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, and Phantoms, but misses Lost Updates and Write Skew (Berenson et al. 1995).

PostgreSQL `REPEATABLE READ` implements **Snapshot Isolation (MVCC)**: readers never block writers, but two transactions reading the same snapshot and writing to *disjoint* rows still cause Write Skew.

PostgreSQL `SERIALIZABLE` uses **SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation)** via SIREAD predicate locks—detecting dangerous `rw`-antidependency cycles without blocking readers, aborting one transaction with SQLSTATE `40001`.

Distributed ACID combines **Two-Phase Commit (2PC)** (or Raft-replicated coordinators) with **Global Ordering**: Spanner uses atomic/GPS clocks (`TrueTime` commit-wait `>= 2ε`, ~7 ms), while CockroachDB uses Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC) + read restarts.
In MySQL InnoDB, `REPEATABLE READ` uses **Next-Key Locks** (record + gap locks) on locking reads (`FOR UPDATE`) to prevent phantoms, which can cause unexpected gap-lock deadlocks.

examples.title: On-Call Doctor Write Skew Under Snapshot Isolation
examples.scenario: A hospital scheduling table requires at least 1 doctor on call. Alice and Bob are both on call. Both open a `REPEATABLE READ` transaction in PostgreSQL, run `SELECT count(*) FROM shifts WHERE on_call = true` (both see `2`), and Alice updates `id = 'alice'` while Bob updates `id = 'bob'` to `on_call = false`.
examples.outcome: Under `REPEATABLE READ`, both commits succeed because they modified disjoint rows—leaving 0 doctors on call. Upgrading the transaction to `SERIALIZABLE` causes PostgreSQL SSI to detect the `rw`-antidependency cycle and abort Bob's commit with `ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions (40001)`.

examples.title: Cross-Shard Ledger Transfer in CockroachDB vs. Spanner
examples.scenario: Transferring $500 from Account A (Shard 1, `us-east`) to Account B (Shard 2, `us-west`) while concurrent balance audits run globally.
examples.outcome: CockroachDB uses parallel 2PC commits with Raft-replicated transaction records and HLC timestamps (~200 ms max offset), guaranteeing `SERIALIZABLE` isolation without GPS hardware, though readers hitting the uncertainty window must restart. Spanner uses `TrueTime` (`TT.now()` with `ε <= 7 ms`) and waits out `2ε` before releasing locks, guaranteeing strict external consistency (linearizable reads).

tradeOffs.pro: `READ COMMITTED` avoids `40001` serialization aborts and maximizes throughput for independent single-row updates.
tradeOffs.con: Requires manual `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` or optimistic version columns (`WHERE version = ?`) on every multi-row invariant, or subtle race conditions slip in.

tradeOffs.factor: Pessimistic Locking (2PL) vs. Optimistic MVCC / SSI
tradeOffs.pro: 2PL (`FOR UPDATE` / InnoDB Next-Key Locks) guarantees the lock holder commits without retrying under high contention.
tradeOffs.con: Writers block readers/writers, risking lock convoys and deadlocks across shards; SSI never blocks readers but aborts conflicting writers at commit time.

tradeOffs.factor: TrueTime Commit-Wait (Spanner) vs. HLC Uncertainty Restarts (CockroachDB)
tradeOffs.pro: Spanner's `2ε` (~7 ms) commit wait gives strict external consistency—if T1 finishes before T2 starts in real time, T2 is guaranteed to see T1.
tradeOffs.con: Adds mandatory ~7–14 ms to every write commit and requires specialized atomic/GPS clocks; HLC runs on commodity NTP VMs at the cost of occasional read restarts.

failureModes.name: Missing `40001` Client Retry Loop
failureModes.description: Enabling `SERIALIZABLE` on PostgreSQL or CockroachDB without application-level retry logic turns normal optimistic concurrency conflicts into HTTP 500 errors.
failureModes.mitigation: Wrap transactions in an idempotent retry loop (max 3–5 attempts with jittered exponential backoff) specifically catching SQLSTATE `40001` (`serialization_failure`) and `40P01` (`deadlock_detected`).

failureModes.name: 2PC Coordinator Blocking
failureModes.description: In classic un-replicated 2PC, if the coordinator crashes after participants vote `PREPARE`, participants hold locks indefinitely until manual intervention.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Raft/Paxos-replicated transaction coordinators (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB) so a new leader immediately resolves `IN_DOUBT` transactions.

failureModes.name: Clock Skew Violating External Consistency
failureModes.description: In HLC-based distributed DBs, if a node's NTP clock drifts beyond `max_offset` (e.g., 500 ms), the node can serve stale reads or crash itself to protect consistency.
failureModes.mitigation: Run local `chrony` with redundant NTP/PTP sources, monitor `clock_offset` metrics, and configure nodes to self-terminate if skew exceeds `max_offset`.

failureModes.name: Long-Running Read Transactions Bloating MVCC & SIREAD Locks
failureModes.description: An analytical query left open for 30 minutes under `REPEATABLE READ` or `SERIALIZABLE` prevents PostgreSQL `VACUUM` from reclaiming dead tuples and accumulates megabytes of SIREAD predicate locks.
failureModes.mitigation: Set `statement_timeout` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` (e.g., 30s) on OLTP pools, and route heavy analytics to a read replica.

commonMistakes: Assuming `REPEATABLE READ` in PostgreSQL prevents Write Skew—it only prevents Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, Phantoms, and Lost Updates.
Catching `40001` serialization errors and retrying *non-idempotent* side effects (like sending an email or charging Stripe) inside the same transaction block.
Using `SELECT * FROM accounts FOR UPDATE` in `READ COMMITTED` without realizing PostgreSQL re-evaluates the `WHERE` clause after waiting on a lock, which can still miss newly inserted rows.
Running `SERIALIZABLE` across hot single-row counters (like `global_sequence_id`), causing 90% abort storms.
Confusing `READ COMMITTED` statement-level snapshots with transaction-level snapshots—two identical `SELECT` queries in the same `READ COMMITTED` transaction can return different rows.

sections.content:
## The idea

**Transaction isolation** defines the illusion a database gives each concurrent transaction: at the strongest level (`SERIALIZABLE`), concurrent transactions produce the exact same final state as if they had executed one-by-one in some serial order.

Weakening isolation boosts concurrency by letting transactions read slightly stale or uncommitted data, but reintroduces **anomalies** (Lost Updates, Phantoms, Write Skew). Extending ACID across **distributed shards** adds two hard constraints: **atomicity** across independent nodes (Two-Phase Commit over Raft) and **global timestamp ordering** without a single bottleneck clock (TrueTime or Hybrid Logical Clocks).

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a distributed `SERIALIZABLE` transfer of $500 from **Account A (Shard 1)** to **Account B (Shard 2)** in a Spanner/CockroachDB-style engine:

1. **Begin & Timestamp**: Coordinator assigns transaction `T1` a read/write timestamp `ts = HLC.now()` (or `TT.now().latest`) and creates a Raft-replicated `PENDING` transaction record.
2. **Parallel Write Intents**: `T1` writes provisional **write intents** (`Account A: -500`, `Account B: +500`) to Shard 1 and Shard 2 via Raft consensus.
3. **2PC Prepare & Conflict Check**: Each shard checks for conflicting `READ` timestamps `> ts` or concurrent write intents. If another transaction `T2` already read Account A at `ts + 1`, Shard 1 rejects `T1` with `40001`.
4. **Commit & Commit-Wait**: Once both shards vote `PREPARED`, the coordinator flips the transaction record to `COMMITTED` via Raft (and in Spanner, waits out `2ε` ~7 ms so `now_real > ts`).
5. **Async Intent Resolution**: `T1` returns `OK` to the client immediately and asynchronously clears the write intent flags on Shards 1 and 2.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Beyond ANSI SQL-92: Lost Updates & Write Skew
sections.content:
## Beyond ANSI SQL-92: Lost Updates & Write Skew

ANSI SQL-92's 3 anomalies (*Dirty Read, Non-Repeatable Read, Phantom Read*) predate MVCC and miss critical concurrency bugs:

- **Lost Update (P4)**: `T1` and `T2` both read `balance = 100`, compute `100 + 20` and `100 + 30`, and overwrite each other—leaving `130` instead of `150`. Prevented by PostgreSQL `REPEATABLE READ` (first-committer-wins abort) and `FOR UPDATE`, but **allowed** in `READ COMMITTED`.
- **Write Skew (A5B)**: `T1` and `T2` read an overlapping set of rows, check an aggregate invariant (`sum >= 0` or `count >= 1`), and update *disjoint* rows. Because MVCC Snapshot Isolation only checks write-write conflicts on the *same* row, both commit. Only `SERIALIZABLE` (SSI) or explicit `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` / materialized lock rows prevent Write Skew.

## Isolation Levels & Anomaly Prevention Matrix

| Isolation Level (Engine) | Dirty Read | Non-Repeatable Read | Phantom Read | Lost Update | Write Skew | Primary Mechanism |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Read Committed** (Postgres) | Prevented | Allowed | Allowed | Allowed | Allowed | Per-statement MVCC snapshot |
| **Repeatable Read** (Postgres) | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | **Allowed** | Transaction-level MVCC Snapshot Isolation |
| **Repeatable Read** (MySQL InnoDB) | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented (locking) | Prevented | **Allowed** (non-locking) | MVCC + Next-Key Locks on `FOR UPDATE` |
| **Serializable** (Postgres SSI) | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | **Prevented** | SIREAD predicate locks + `40001` aborts |
| **External Consistency** (Spanner) | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | **Prevented** | 2PL + 2PC + TrueTime `2ε` commit-wait |

## Failure modes

1. **Convoy Effect on Hot Keys**: Under 2PL (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`), 200 concurrent threads updating the same merchant balance form a serial queue; if each takes 15 ms, the 200th waits 3 seconds and triggers client timeouts.
2. **SSI False-Positive Aborts**: PostgreSQL's SIREAD locks track page/tuple granularity; heavy concurrent inserts on the same B-tree leaf page can trigger `40001` aborts even between logically disjoint transactions.
3. **Cross-Region RTT Amplification**: Synchronous 2PC + Raft across 3 continents adds 80–150 ms per commit, collapsing single-key throughput to ~10 TPS unless batched or localized via geo-partitioning.

## Choosing a Distributed ACID Strategy

- **When you need global linearizable reads**: Use **Google Spanner** (`TrueTime`) or **CockroachDB** (`SERIALIZABLE` with geo-partitioned leaseholders) so stale reads never occur after a commit.
- **When you need high write throughput on contended keys**: Consider **Deterministic Databases (Calvin / Fauna-style)** that sequence all transaction inputs via Raft *before* execution, eliminating 2PC prepare round-trips and aborts—at the cost of requiring all read/write keys to be known upfront.
- **When crossing service boundaries**: Never stretch 2PC/XA across independent microservices; keep ACID local to each service's database and bridge services asynchronously with the **Transactional Outbox**.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Audit every `READ COMMITTED` read-modify-write path for Lost Updates (`FOR UPDATE` or atomic `UPDATE ... WHERE`).
- [ ] Use `SERIALIZABLE` (or explicit parent-row locking) whenever an invariant spans multiple rows (e.g., quotas, shifts, ledgers).
- [ ] Implement an idempotent retry wrapper for SQLSTATE `40001` / `40P01` with jittered backoff.
- [ ] Keep transactions short: never make external HTTP calls (Stripe, SMTP) inside an open DB transaction.
- [ ] Enforce `statement_timeout` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` to protect MVCC vacuuming.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Transaction Isolation Distributed Acid

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Isolation levels control which concurrent read/write anomalies a database permits, trading throughput and lock/abort rates for correctness—while distributed ACID extends those guarantees across shards via 2PC, TrueTime, or HLCs.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Shard 1 (Raft) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Shard 2 (Raft).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Shard 2 (Raft) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Wrap transactions in an idempotent retry loop (max 3–5 attempts with jittered exponential backoff) specifically catching SQLSTATE `40001` (`serialization_failure`) and `40P01` (`deadlock_detected`).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ is Snapshot Isolation (still vulnerable to Write Skew), not true Serializability; across shards, distributed ACID requires either 2PC + SSI/TrueTime commit-wait or deterministic ordering—and retry loops for 40001 serialization failures.
Avoid trap: Assuming `REPEATABLE READ` in PostgreSQL prevents Write Skew—it only prevents Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, Phantoms, and Lost Updates.
Avoid trap: Catching `40001` serialization errors and retrying *non-idempotent* side effects (like sending an email or charging Stripe) inside the same transaction block.
When to reach for it: Financial ledgers, double-entry accounting, and inventory/seat reservations where lost updates, phantom reads, or write skew violate business invariants.
When to reach for it: Multi-shard writes in CockroachDB, Google Spanner, or YugabyteDB where cross-partition atomicity and external consistency (linearizability) are required.

putItTogether.title: Putting Transaction Isolation Distributed Acid Together
putItTogether.summary: PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ is Snapshot Isolation (still vulnerable to Write Skew), not true Serializability; across shards, distributed ACID requires either 2PC + SSI/TrueTime commit-wait or deterministic ordering—and retry loops for 40001 serialization failures.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Transaction Isolation Distributed Acid before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Under `REPEATABLE READ`, both commits succeed because they modified disjoint rows—leaving 0 doctors on call. Upgrading the transaction to `SERIALIZABLE` causes PostgreSQL SSI to detect the `rw`-antidependency cycle and abort Bob's commit with `ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions (40001)`.
